message: Function "<anonymous>" uses user input in a file system operation without path sanitization.
fix: Use path.basename() to strip directory components, then verify: "if (!resolved.startsWith(ALLOWED_DIR)) return 403".

attackPath: Attacker sends GET /files/download with file set to a traversal payload such as ../../etc/passwd.
Handler joins attacker-controlled req.query.file onto UPLOADS with no sanitization or allowlist.
Express returns the file at the escaped path via res.sendFile.
reasoning.impact: Attacker can read arbitrary files the server process can access outside the uploads directory, including system files and secrets.
reasoning.fixSummary: Resolve the joined path and reject unless it stays inside UPLOADS, or only allow known filenames via path.basename allowlist.
reasoning.plainLanguage: Anyone on the internet can trick the download link to read private files from your server. This matters because leaked secrets and user files could be used to break in further and harm your users.

message: Shell command with user input — command injection risk
fix: Sanitize all user input before use. For HTML: use a sanitization library or textContent instead of innerHTML. For SQL: use parameterized queries. For shell: use allowlists, never interpolate user input into commands.

message: exec() runs a shell command built from interpolated input — if any of it is user-controlled, that's remote code execution (a "; rm -rf" away).
fix: Never build a shell command from input. Use execFile()/spawn() with the program and an ARGUMENT ARRAY (no `shell: true`) so args can't break out: `execFile("convert", [userFile, out])`. If a value must reach a shell, strictly allowlist it.

attackPath: Attacker sends unauthenticated GET request to /network/ping with a hostile host query value containing shell metacharacters.
Server handler interpolates req.query.host directly into a shell command string with no validation or escaping.
exec() runs the combined string in a system shell, executing the attacker's injected commands with server privileges.
reasoning.impact: Attacker gets remote code execution on the server as the Node.js user, allowing reading or changing app data and running arbitrary system commands.
reasoning.fixSummary: Replace exec() with execFile('ping', ['-c','1', host]) so host is passed as an argument without a shell, and validate host as IP or hostname.
reasoning.plainLanguage: Anyone on the internet can send a crafted web address to this ping feature and make the server run their own commands. That matters because they could steal information, break the service, or take over the computer running your app.

message: Function "<anonymous>" fetches a user-provided URL without validation — SSRF risk.
fix: Validate URL: parse with new URL(), verify protocol is https, block private IP ranges, optionally allowlist domains.

message: Function "<anonymous>" uses a user-supplied ID without verifying ownership in the same function scope.
evidence: const rows = await db.query(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${req.params.id}`);
fix: After extracting the ID, verify ownership within the same function: "if (resource.userId !== session.user.id) return 403".

attackPath: Attacker sends an unauthenticated GET request to /users/2 to request another user's record.
Server uses the request id value directly in the database lookup without checking who owns it.
Server returns the other user's database row as JSON to the attacker.
reasoning.impact: Attacker can read any user's stored record by changing the id in the URL.

evidence.quote: // Anyone can call this, and the id is pasted straight into the SQL text.
const rows = await db.query(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${req.params.id}`);

reasoning.fixSummary: Require login and verify the requested id belongs to the logged-in user before querying, rejecting other ids with forbidden.
reasoning.plainLanguage: Anyone can change the number in the profile address to see another person's private account information. This loss of privacy can drive customers away and create legal costs for the business.

message: Function "<anonymous>" uses a user-supplied ID without verifying ownership in the same function scope.
evidence: await db.query('DELETE FROM users WHERE id = ' + req.params.id);
fix: After extracting the ID, verify ownership within the same function: "if (resource.userId !== session.user.id) return 403".

attackPath: Attacker sends an anonymous DELETE request to /users/<victim-id>.
Express delivers it to the users router mounted at /users with only JSON parsing and no login check.
Handler deletes the database row for the attacker-supplied ID without verifying ownership.
reasoning.impact: Attacker can delete any user account without logging in by supplying its ID, causing permanent account loss and lockout.

evidence.quote: await db.query('DELETE FROM users WHERE id = ' + req.params.id);
// Anyone can delete any account. No check on who is asking.

reasoning.fixSummary: Require authentication on DELETE /users/:id and verify the caller owns the ID or has an admin role, returning 403 otherwise.
reasoning.plainLanguage: Anyone on the internet can delete any customer account just by guessing its number, with no password needed. This would lock real users out and quickly destroy trust in your business.

message: SQL query built with template-literal interpolation — user input can rewrite the query.
evidence: const rows = await db.query(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${req.params.id}`);
fix: Use parameterized queries / prepared statements. Pass values as a separate argument, never build the SQL string with `+` or `${}`. Examples: pg — client.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1", [id]); mysql2 — conn.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?", [id]); Prisma/Drizzle — use the query builder or sql`...${id}` tagged templates that bind safely.

attackPath: Attacker sends unauthenticated GET request to /users/:id with SQL payload in the id segment.
Express forwards the request to the usersRouter handler mounted at /users with no auth check.
Handler pastes req.params.id directly into SQL text and executes it via db.query then returns the result.
reasoning.impact: Attacker can rewrite the WHERE clause to bypass the id lookup and read arbitrary rows from the users table.

evidence.quote: // Anyone can call this, and the id is pasted straight into the SQL text.
const rows = await db.query(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${req.params.id}`);

reasoning.fixSummary: Use a parameterized query such as db.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1', [req.params.id]) and validate id is numeric.
reasoning.plainLanguage: Anyone on the internet can ask for one user account and trick the system into showing private details for many other accounts. Losing control of customer details like this can break trust and create legal and money problems for the business.

message: SQL query built with string concatenation — user input can rewrite the query.
evidence: await db.query('DELETE FROM users WHERE id = ' + req.params.id);
fix: Use parameterized queries / prepared statements. Pass values as a separate argument, never build the SQL string with `+` or `${}`. Examples: pg — client.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1", [id]); mysql2 — conn.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?", [id]); Prisma/Drizzle — use the query builder or sql`...${id}` tagged templates that bind safely.

attackPath: Attacker sends an unauthenticated DELETE request to /users/:id with a crafted id value.
The delete handler concatenates req.params.id directly into the DELETE statement with no parameterization.
The database executes the rewritten query, allowing deletion of arbitrary or all users.
reasoning.impact: An attacker can delete any user account and can rewrite the query to delete all users or alter database logic, e.g. with `0 OR 1=1`.

evidence.quote: await db.query('DELETE FROM users WHERE id = ' + req.params.id);
// Anyone can delete any account. No check on who is asking.

reasoning.fixSummary: Use a parameterized query such as db.query('DELETE FROM users WHERE id = $1', [req.params.id]) and require authorization for deletes.
reasoning.plainLanguage: Anyone on the internet can delete any customer account by sending a specially shaped web address, and can even wipe out every account at once. Losing all user accounts would break trust with customers and shut down the business.

message: State-changing route with no CSRF protection
fix: Add CSRF protection to state-changing endpoints. Options: (1) Use SameSite=Lax or Strict cookies. (2) Implement double-submit cookie pattern. (3) Check Origin/Referer headers. (4) Use a CSRF token library like csrf-csrf. Without CSRF protection, attackers can trigger actions on behalf of your users from external sites.

message: SQL SELECT without LIMIT clause — returns all matching rows
evidence: const rows = await db.query(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${req.params.id}`);
fix: Always add pagination or limits to list endpoints. Use limit/offset, cursor-based pagination, or at minimum a hard cap (e.g., .limit(100)). Without limits: (1) anyone can scrape your entire database in one request, (2) large result sets crash your server or client, (3) it's a trivial DoS vector.

message: No error monitoring/alerting dependency found (Sentry, Rollbar, Bugsnag, Datadog…). Production errors will fail silently — you won't know the app is broken until a user tells you.
fix: Add an error monitor: @sentry/nextjs (or @sentry/node), Rollbar, or Bugsnag — wire it to capture unhandled errors and alert you. If your host already provides this, treat this as informational.
